opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun. It's great to be here.

When I talk about AGI, I usually break it into three layers. The first is information intelligence: language models, search, content generation, coding. That's where we've seen the most dramatic progress, and I think we're already fairly close to what you could call AGI in that digital domain, maybe within about five years for it to be broadly mature.

The second layer is physical intelligence. That's when intelligence moves out of the screen and into the real world: autonomous vehicles, robots, drones, factories, logistics. The third is biological intelligence, connecting AI with the human body and life sciences, things like brain-computer interfaces and AI-driven drug discovery. That one will take even longer.

So when I say physical AGI will take about ten years to become mainstream, I mean a few things. First, the physical world is much harder than the digital world. In language you can make mistakes and simply regenerate the answer. On the road or in a factory, a mistake can cost lives. The bar for safety and reliability is orders of magnitude higher. Second, data is scarcer. The internet gave us trillions of tokens of text, but we don't have an equivalent internet of physical interaction. We have to build it through simulation, world models, and large-scale real-world deployment, and that takes time. Third, hardware has its own cycle. Sensors, actuators, batteries, and chips don't improve on software timelines, and cost has to come down before anything goes mass market.

Take autonomous driving as an example. I believe it will be the first large-scale application of physical AGI. We're already seeing robotaxis operating commercially in several cities. But going from tens of thousands of vehicles to a meaningful share of all cars on the road, with the regulation, insurance, and public trust that requires, is a roughly ten-year process. Humanoid and general-purpose robots will follow, probably somewhat later.

So "mainstream" is the key word. I don't mean the technology won't work until then. I mean it takes about a decade for it to be safe, affordable, and widely deployed enough to become part of everyday life.

r001.rationale: The response describes mainstream adoption as safe, affordable, and widely deployed enough to be part of everyday life, but does not define it as practical availability for ordinary household use.

r002.rationale: The response discusses robotaxis and future humanoid robots, but does not distinguish research or teaching robots from mainstream products serving end users.

fable-5.1.text:
When I say AGI in the physical world will take about ten years to become mainstream, I'm making a distinction between three stages of AGI, and the physical stage is the hardest one.

The first stage is information intelligence. That's the digital world: language models, code, images, video, the things we're seeing explode right now. In that domain I think we'll reach something you could call AGI within two to three years. The data is abundant, the feedback loops are fast, and the cost of making a mistake is low. If a model writes a bad paragraph, you just regenerate it.

The second stage is physical intelligence, or what some people call embodied AI. This is autonomous driving, robots, drones, humanoids, machines that have to perceive, decide, and act in the real world. Here the problems are fundamentally different. You don't have trillions of tokens of clean training data lying around on the internet. You have to collect data from sensors, from the real world, and that's slow and expensive. The environment is open, with long-tail situations that nobody anticipated. And the cost of error is very high. A car that is 99 percent correct is not a product, it's a liability. So you need reliability levels that are orders of magnitude beyond what's acceptable in a chatbot.

On top of that, you have the hardware constraints. Models have to run on the edge with limited compute and power. You have to integrate perception, planning, and control into one system. And then there's the whole industrial chain: manufacturing, supply chains, cost reduction, regulation, insurance, safety standards. Even when the technology works, it takes years for it to scale and for society to accept it. Look at autonomous driving. The technology has been "almost there" for a decade, and only now are we seeing robotaxis operating at some scale in a few cities.

So when I say ten years, I mean it's a gradual process. You'll see pockets of it earlier, in logistics, in factories, in specific vertical applications. But for physical AGI to be mainstream, meaning robots and autonomous systems are a normal part of daily life, the way smartphones are, I think we're looking at around 2035.

And then there's a third stage, which is biological intelligence, where AI connects with the human body and the brain, through brain-computer interfaces and so on. That's even further out, maybe fifteen to twenty years. So ten years isn't pessimistic. It's actually quite ambitious, given how much has to happen between now and then.

r001.rationale: The response says physical AGI will become a normal part of daily life, but does not define mainstream availability specifically as practical use in ordinary households.

r002.rationale: It contrasts early use in logistics, factories, and vertical applications with mainstream adoption, but does not distinguish research or teaching robots from products that directly serve end users.

astra-6.text:
What I mean is that there is a difference between AI that can answer questions and AI that can act reliably in the physical world. A system may understand your instruction, but a robot also has to perceive its surroundings, plan its movements, and handle unexpected situations safely.

Think about asking a robot to clean your kitchen. Every kitchen is different. Objects move, something may spill, a child may walk into the room. The robot has to adapt to all of that. And to become mainstream, it has to do so consistently, at a cost people can afford.

So ten years is an estimate of the time needed for those capabilities to become widely useful and deployed. It doesn't mean we wait ten years to see progress. We will see applications earlier in more controlled environments. The longer journey is toward machines that can operate across many different tasks and environments with very little human intervention.

r001.rationale: The kitchen-cleaning example, consistent operation, affordability, and wide deployment together define mainstream status as practical household use.

r002.rationale: The response does not distinguish research or teaching robots from products that directly serve end users.

sol-6.1.text:
What I mean is that there’s a difference between intelligence in the digital world and intelligence that can act reliably in the physical world. A system can generate text or write code, but for a robot to work in your home, it has to perceive its surroundings, understand what’s happening, plan an action, and execute it safely. All of those capabilities have to work together.

And the physical world is much less forgiving. If you give a poor answer, you can try again. If you move an object incorrectly, you might break it or hurt someone. So reliability, safety, hardware, and cost all become very important.

Ten years is a rough estimate for broad adoption, not a precise deadline. We’ll see useful applications earlier, particularly in environments where the tasks are well defined. But getting to general-purpose systems that ordinary people can afford and trust in everyday life—that will take longer. That’s what I mean by mainstream.

r001.rationale: It defines mainstream as general-purpose systems ordinary people can afford and trust for everyday life, and gives working in the home as an example.

r002.rationale: It does not distinguish robots used for research or teaching from products that directly serve end users.
